teaching.causalExplanation: In twenty fifteen, all one hundred and ninety-three United Nations member states adopted the Sustainable Development Goals: seventeen goals, with one hundred and sixty-nine targets, to be reached by twenty thirty. They replaced eight Millennium Development Goals, and four things changed. They apply to every country, not just poor ones, so Australia reports on itself. They're integrated, not separate. They gave the environment far more weight, and added inequality. And they promise to leave no one behind: progress must reach the most disadvantaged, not just lift the average. Goal three is good health and well-being: healthy lives and well-being for all, at all ages. Its targets include cutting maternal and child deaths, ending epidemics like AIDS and malaria, reducing early deaths from non-communicable diseases by a third and promoting mental health, halving road traffic deaths, and universal health coverage. For Australia, the chronic disease, mental health and road targets matter most. Treat the goals as something only for other countries, and you've missed the point. Health appears once in the goal titles, and everywhere in the mechanisms. The other goals name the determinants of health almost one by one. No poverty: income decides housing, food and whether care is delayed. Zero hunger: early nutrition shapes growth and lifelong disease risk. Clean water: diarrhoea still kills young children, and much of it is prevented by safe water and sanitation, not by clinics alone. Decent work: secure income and safe workplaces. Reduced inequalities: health follows social position. And climate action: heat, smoke and disaster. Lay them beside the determinants, and the match is close to one to one.

scenes.teachingReason: So here's the case for Proposal B, the SDG argument in one budget. A girl who finishes secondary school tends to have her first child later, has fewer and better-spaced pregnancies, can read health information and use vaccination services, and has more income and more say in household spending. That's indivisibility: the goals can't be achieved separately. It's the socio-ecological approach, written as a global agreement.

scenes.teachingReason: The syllabus asks how the World Health Organization applies a health lens, and it uses the goals four ways. As a measuring framework: it looks after many health indicators and publishes progress, which makes failure visible. As an argument for universal health coverage, everyone getting needed care without financial hardship. As the basis for health in all policies, where transport, housing and education departments weigh the health effects of their decisions. And for equity: leave no one behind means reporting results separately by group. But the goals aren't law. Nobody's penalised for missing them. They coordinate and make failure visible, and advocates use that.
